claims.text: In equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles, increased local atomic disorder reduces local cohesive energy.
Heterogeneous bonding environments and enhanced lattice strain mediate the reduction in cohesive energy associated with local atomic disorder.
Reduced local cohesive energy lowers the local premelting temperature.
Enhanced local chemical ordering raises the local energy threshold for melting.
The onset and temperature range of premelting are governed by the degree of local atomic order.
Rapid quenching increases atomic disorder relative to moderate post-annealing.
Moderate post-annealing promotes local atomic ordering without significant grain growth.
Regions with high local atomic disorder contain atomic-size and bonding-environment mismatches.
Disordered regions with reduced cohesive energy act as nucleation centers for premelting.
Locally ordered regions have more uniform bonding environments and higher cohesive energy than disordered regions.
Higher cohesive energy in locally ordered regions delays the onset of premelting.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will begin surface premelting earlier than annealed nanoparticles.
The surface-premelting onset of rapidly quenched nanoparticles may be 20–30 °C lower than that of annealed nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting-temperature range than annealed nanoparticles.
Annealed, locally ordered nanoparticles will have a higher and sharper melting onset than rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
Nearly identical melting behavior in the quenched and annealed groups would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in premelting onset beyond experimental uncertainty in the quenched group would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to correlate melting differences with verified differences in local atomic order and strain would falsify the hypothesis.
The proposed relationship may not extend to non-equiatomic compositions, substantially different particle sizes, or alternative environments.
